bss.topic: Imigração europeia e o trabalho livre

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual foi o principal produto agrícola que atraiu imigrantes europeus para São Paulo no século XIX?
questions.hint: Pense nas grandes fazendas do Oeste Paulista.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama o trabalho em que a pessoa recebe pagamento e não é propriedade de ninguém, que substituiu aos poucos a escravidão?
questions.hint: É o contrário do trabalho escravizado.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano foi aprovada a Lei de Terras no Brasil?
questions.hint: Foi no mesmo ano da lei que proibiu o tráfico de africanos escravizados.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que a Lei de Terras de 1850 determinou?
options: As terras públicas só poderiam ser obtidas por compra
Todo imigrante ganharia um lote de graça
As terras seriam divididas entre os escravizados libertos
A Igreja passaria a controlar as terras
questions.answer: As terras públicas só poderiam ser obtidas por compra
questions.hint: Pense em quem tinha dinheiro para comprar terra.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que a Lei de Terras dificultou que imigrantes pobres e ex-escravizados se tornassem proprietários?
options: Porque eles não tinham dinheiro para comprar terras
Porque eles eram proibidos de trabalhar no campo
Porque só podiam morar nas cidades
Porque as terras eram todas da Coroa portuguesa
questions.answer: Porque eles não tinham dinheiro para comprar terras
questions.hint: A terra virou mercadoria.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual lei de 1850 proibiu o tráfico de africanos escravizados para o Brasil?
questions.hint: Tem o nome de um ministro da época.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano a Lei Áurea aboliu a escravidão no Brasil?
questions.hint: Foi um ano antes da Proclamação da República.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: No sistema de parceria, como o imigrante pagava a viagem e as despesas iniciais?
options: Ficava endividado com o fazendeiro e pagava com o trabalho
O governo pagava tudo e ele não devia nada
Ele já chegava com a viagem paga pela família
Trabalhava de graça só no primeiro mês
questions.answer: Ficava endividado com o fazendeiro e pagava com o trabalho
questions.hint: Pense em por que muitos parceiros se revoltaram.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que o sistema de parceria fracassou?
options: Os imigrantes ficavam presos a dívidas e havia conflitos com os fazendeiros
Os fazendeiros pagavam salários altos demais
O café deixou de ser vendido
Os imigrantes recusavam-se a plantar alimentos
questions.answer: Os imigrantes ficavam presos a dívidas e havia conflitos com os fazendeiros
questions.hint: Houve revoltas, como a da fazenda Ibicaba.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: De que países vinham principalmente os parceiros da revolta na fazenda Ibicaba, nos anos 1850?
questions.hint: Eram imigrantes da Europa central.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual sistema de trabalho substituiu a parceria nas fazendas de café, com pagamento fixo pelo cuidado dos cafeeiros e mais um valor pela colheita?
questions.hint: O trabalhador era chamado de colono.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destes direitos o colono costumava ter no colonato?
options: Plantar alimentos para a família entre os pés de café
Ficar com metade da fazenda depois de 5 anos
Não trabalhar na época da colheita
questions.answer: Plantar alimentos para a família entre os pés de café
questions.hint: Isso ajudava a família a se alimentar.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual grupo de imigrantes europeus foi o mais numeroso nas fazendas de café paulistas no fim do século XIX?
questions.hint: Muitos vieram fugindo de crises no próprio país.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que o governo da província de São Paulo passou a pagar as passagens dos imigrantes a partir dos anos 1880?
options: Para garantir mão de obra para o café com o fim da escravidão próximo
questions.answer: Para garantir mão de obra para o café com o fim da escravidão próximo
questions.hint: Pense no que estava acontecendo com a escravidão nessa década.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique por que muitos ex-escravizados não foram contratados como trabalhadores livres nas fazendas após 1888 e quais foram as consequências disso.
questions.hint: Pense na preferência dos fazendeiros, no racismo e na falta de acesso à terra.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Compare o sistema de parceria e o colonato: o que mudou para o trabalhador imigrante?
questions.hint: Pense em dívidas, forma de pagamento e direito de plantar.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is the key idea of the von Neumann architecture?
options: Instructions and data are stored in the same memory
Instructions and data are stored in separate memories
Programs are stored only on paper
questions.answer: Instructions and data are stored in the same memory
questions.hint: It is often called the 'stored program' concept.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.hint: Its name says it keeps count through the program.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register stores the results of calculations carried out by the ALU?
questions.hint: It accumulates results.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What does MAR stand for?
questions.hint: It holds an address, not data.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register temporarily holds data or an instruction that has just been read from, or is about to be written to, memory?
questions.hint: Think 'data', not 'address'.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which register holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed?
questions.hint: The word 'current' is a clue.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which part of the CPU carries out arithmetic and logical operations?
questions.hint: Its name includes 'arithmetic'.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is the main job of the Control Unit?
options: To decode instructions and coordinate the other components
To display output on the screen
questions.answer: To decode instructions and coordinate the other components
questions.hint: It sends control signals.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which bus carries memory addresses from the CPU to main memory?
questions.hint: The name tells you what it carries.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which bus is one-way (unidirectional)?
questions.hint: Only the CPU sends locations to memory.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Put the stages of the cycle in the correct order.
questions.hint: The CPU must get the instruction before understanding it.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: During the fetch stage, what happens straight after the address in the PC is copied to the MAR?
questions.hint: The PC must get ready for the next instruction.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A program counter currently holds the value 104. Instructions are fetched one after another with no jumps. What value will the PC hold after three more instructions have been fetched?
questions.hint: Each fetch adds 1.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is meant by the 'von Neumann bottleneck'?
options: Instructions and data share one bus, which limits speed
The CPU has too many registers
The screen is slower than the keyboard
questions.answer: Instructions and data share one bus, which limits speed
questions.hint: Think about traffic on a single road.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Describe what happens to the PC, MAR, MDR and CIR during the fetch stage of the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
questions.hint: Follow the address from the PC to memory and the instruction back to the CIR.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of storing both instructions and data in the same memory.
questions.hint: Think about flexibility versus the shared pathway.

en.topic: Reading non-fiction: explicit and implicit information

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is explicit information in a text?
options: Information you have to work out from clues
questions.hint: 'Explicit' means clearly expressed.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is implicit information?
options: Information suggested but not stated directly
A list of facts at the end of a text
questions.answer: Information suggested but not stated directly
questions.hint: You need to read between the lines.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which word means to find and take information directly from a text?
questions.hint: It begins with 're-'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which word means to work out a meaning from clues in a text?
questions.hint: It is the skill of 'reading between the lines'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which of these is a non-fiction text?
options: A newspaper report about a flood
A fairy tale about a dragon
A poem about an imaginary island
A short story about a talking cat
questions.answer: A newspaper report about a flood
questions.hint: Non-fiction is about real events and facts.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'The museum opens at 9 a.m. and closes at 5 p.m. on weekdays.' What time does the museum close on weekdays?
questions.hint: This is stated directly.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'After the storm, the town hall's roof lay in the car park.' What can you infer?
options: The town hall was being repaired
questions.hint: Think about what force would be needed.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'By the third hour of the hike, Maya's water bottle was empty and her steps were getting slower.' What can you infer about Maya?
options: She was becoming tired and thirsty
She was enjoying a quick walk
She had brought too much water
questions.answer: She was becoming tired and thirsty
questions.hint: Look at both clues together.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'Tickets sold out within ten minutes of going on sale.' What does this imply about the event?
questions.hint: Think about why tickets would go so quickly.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'The volunteers worked through the night, refusing to stop until every sandbag was in place.' Which quality does this imply the volunteers had?
questions.hint: Look at the phrase 'refusing to stop'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which statement is explicit information from this sentence: 'The bridge, built in 1902, carries over 40,000 vehicles a day'?
questions.hint: Choose what is actually written.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'Despite the rain, the queue for the new café stretched round the block.' What can you infer?
options: People were very keen to try the café
The café was very small inside
questions.answer: People were very keen to try the café
questions.hint: Why would people wait in the rain?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'The old factory's windows were boarded up and weeds pushed through the cracked tarmac.' What can you infer about the factory?
options: It has been abandoned for some time
questions.answer: It has been abandoned for some time
questions.hint: Weeds take time to grow.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: When you make an inference in an exam answer, what should you always include?
options: Evidence from the text to support it
A summary of the whole text
Your favourite quotation from another book
A list of the writer's techniques only
questions.answer: Evidence from the text to support it
questions.hint: Show how you know.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'Every morning, Mr Hale's dog waits by the gate at exactly 7.45, its tail already wagging before the school bus appears.' What can you infer about the dog's routine? Support your answer with evidence.
questions.hint: Use the time and the dog's behaviour as clues.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Read: 'The charity's shelves, once full, now held only a few tins of beans and a single packet of pasta.' What does this suggest about the charity's situation, and how do you know?
questions.hint: Compare 'once full' with 'now'.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What does 'evaluate' mean in a reading question?
options: Judge how effective or convincing something is
questions.answer: Judge how effective or convincing something is
questions.hint: It involves making a judgement.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: A 'to what extent' question asks you to:
options: Decide how far you agree, weighing different sides
questions.answer: Decide how far you agree, weighing different sides
questions.hint: Your answer can be 'partly'.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What is the word for a reasoned decision you reach after considering evidence?
questions.hint: It is what a judge makes.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which phrase best shows a balanced evaluation?
options: To some extent I agree, because…, however…
This is the best text ever written.
questions.answer: To some extent I agree, because…, however…
questions.hint: Look for both sides.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What is the best evidence to support a point about a text?
options: A short, relevant quotation from the text
A long copy of the whole paragraph
A guess about the writer's life
questions.answer: A short, relevant quotation from the text
questions.hint: Precise and relevant is best.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: A student wants to argue against the statement. What should they do?
options: Find evidence that challenges it and explain why
Repeat the statement in capital letters
questions.answer: Find evidence that challenges it and explain why
questions.hint: Counter-evidence needs explaining too.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Statement: 'The writer presents the city as a frightening place.' Which quotation best SUPPORTS this?
options: 'Shadows crept along the alleys like hungry animals.'
questions.answer: 'Shadows crept along the alleys like hungry animals.'
questions.hint: Which image creates fear?

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Statement: 'The writer presents the city as a frightening place.' Which quotation best CHALLENGES this?
questions.hint: Look for a positive image.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which word shows that a reader is making a tentative (not certain) judgement?
questions.hint: It suggests possibility.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which sentence is the best start to a critical evaluation?
options: I largely agree with this statement because the writer's imagery repeatedly creates tension.
This text is about a city.
questions.answer: I largely agree with this statement because the writer's imagery repeatedly creates tension.
questions.hint: It gives a clear judgement and a reason.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What does 'critical' mean in 'critical reading'?
options: Thinking carefully and questioning what you read
questions.answer: Thinking carefully and questioning what you read
questions.hint: It is not the same as complaining.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: In an evaluation, why is it useful to comment on the effect of a word on the reader?
options: It explains how the evidence supports your judgement
It shows you know the writer's age
questions.answer: It explains how the evidence supports your judgement
questions.hint: Evidence needs explanation.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which connective is best for introducing a counter-argument?
questions.hint: It signals a contrast.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which is the most effective conclusion to a 'to what extent' answer?
options: A clear final judgement that sums up how far you agree and why
A new quotation not discussed before
A list of all the paragraphs
questions.answer: A clear final judgement that sums up how far you agree and why
questions.hint: End with your overall decision.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Statement: 'Reading books is more valuable than watching films.' To what extent do you agree? Give one reason for and one against, then your judgement.
questions.hint: Weigh both sides before deciding.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: A student wrote: 'The writer makes the storm seem exciting.' Suggest one piece of evidence a writer might use to support this and explain its effect.
questions.hint: Think of a vivid verb or image linked to energy.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: What does « le mariage » mean in English?
questions.hint: Think of a ceremony where two people promise to stay together.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Translate into French: the party (use the article).
questions.hint: It is a feminine noun; the verb « fêter » comes from it.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: « L'Aïd » is a festival celebrated mainly by which group of people?
questions.hint: It marks the end of Ramadan.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Choose the correct verb: « Nous ___ l'anniversaire de ma sœur samedi dernier. »
questions.hint: « Samedi dernier » tells you it is in the past; « fêter » takes avoir.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Translate into French: to invite
questions.hint: It looks very similar to the English word.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Which sentence is in the near future (futur proche)?
questions.hint: The near future uses « aller » + infinitive.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Put into the passé composé (je form): « je danse ». Write the whole verb phrase.
questions.hint: Use the present of « avoir » + past participle ending in -é.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Choose the correct form: « Ma grand-mère ___ à la fête en retard. »
questions.hint: « Arriver » takes être, so the participle agrees with a feminine subject.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: What does « Pendant l'Aïd, on mange des gâteaux et on rend visite à la famille » mean?
options: During Eid, people eat cakes and visit family.
Before Eid, people buy cakes for the family.
After Eid, the family makes cakes at home.
During Eid, people do not eat cakes.
questions.answer: During Eid, people eat cakes and visit family.
questions.hint: « Pendant » = during; « rendre visite à » = to visit someone.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Translate into French using the simple future (futur simple): we will celebrate
questions.hint: Take the infinitive and add the ending for « nous »: -ons.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Which word completes the sentence? « Le jour de mon anniversaire, j'ai reçu beaucoup de ___. »
questions.hint: You receive these on your birthday; it must be a plural noun.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: « Les mariés » are…
questions.hint: It comes from « se marier » — the people getting married.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: L'année prochaine, nous irons au mariage de mon oncle.
L'année prochaine, nous sommes allés au mariage de mon oncle.
L'année dernière, nous irons au mariage de mon oncle.
L'année prochaine, nous allions au mariage de mon oncle.
questions.answer: L'année prochaine, nous irons au mariage de mon oncle.
questions.hint: Match the time phrase to the tense.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Translate into French: last year (two words)
questions.hint: It is a time phrase that signals the passé composé.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: « J'ai invité vingt amis et nous avons dansé jusqu'à minuit. » Which tense is used?
questions.hint: Look at the auxiliary « ai/avons » + past participle.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Write 2–3 sentences in French about a celebration: say what you did last time (passé composé) and what you will do next time (futur proche or futur simple).
questions.hint: Use phrases like « l'année dernière, j'ai… » and « l'année prochaine, je vais… ».

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: What does HIC stand for?
questions.hint: It is a way of grouping countries by wealth.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: What word describes land that has been built on before and can be redeveloped?
questions.hint: It is the opposite of greenfield.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: What is deindustrialisation?
options: The decline of manufacturing industry in an area
The growth of factories in a city
The movement of people from cities to farms
The building of new houses on farmland
questions.answer: The decline of manufacturing industry in an area
questions.hint: Think about factories and docks closing.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which term means improving a run-down area through investment in housing, jobs and services?
questions.hint: The word contains 'generate' — making something new again.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Why did London's docks decline in the 1960s and 1970s?
options: Larger container ships could not reach them easily
Trade with other countries stopped completely
The docks were moved to Scotland
questions.answer: Larger container ships could not reach them easily
questions.hint: Think about how shipping changed size and method.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which area of East London, once full of docks, became the site of a major financial district at Canary Wharf? (one word)
questions.hint: The name describes what used to be there.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: What is gentrification?
options: Wealthier people moving into a poorer area and improving it
People leaving the city for the countryside
questions.answer: Wealthier people moving into a poorer area and improving it
questions.hint: It often changes who lives in a neighbourhood and how much homes cost.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which is a likely negative effect of gentrification for long-term residents?
questions.hint: Think about who can still afford to live there.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which light railway was built in the 1980s to improve transport in the regenerated Docklands?
questions.hint: Its name includes the area it serves.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: The 2012 Olympic Park was built mainly on brownfield land in which part of London?
questions.hint: It is in the east, near the old industrial Lower Lea Valley.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Why do planners often prefer building on brownfield sites?
options: It protects the countryside from urban sprawl
It is always cheaper than greenfield land
It is always far from existing services
questions.answer: It protects the countryside from urban sprawl
questions.hint: Think about what happens to green space if cities keep spreading.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which statement best describes a 'flagship' regeneration project?
options: A large, high-profile development meant to attract further investment
A small community garden run by volunteers
A plan to close old factories
A rule that stops new building
questions.answer: A large, high-profile development meant to attract further investment
questions.hint: It is meant to lead the way, like the leading ship of a fleet.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Which group was most likely to lose out when the London docks closed?
options: Dock workers who lost their jobs
questions.answer: Dock workers who lost their jobs
questions.hint: Consider who depended on the docks for income.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: What is the opposite of brownfield land: land that has never been built on?
questions.hint: Think of the colour of fields in the countryside.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the regeneration of London Docklands for local people.
questions.hint: Think about jobs, housing, transport and who could afford to live there.

questions.subject: geog
questions.q: Explain how deindustrialisation can lead to the need for regeneration in a city.
questions.hint: Start with what happens to jobs and buildings when factories or docks close.

hist.topic: Appeasement and the road to the Second World War

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: What was appeasement?
options: Giving in to some demands to avoid war
Building up armies to attack first
Forming a military alliance against Germany
Refusing to talk to other countries
questions.answer: Giving in to some demands to avoid war
questions.hint: Think about the word 'appease' — to calm someone down.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Who was the British Prime Minister most associated with appeasement in 1938?
questions.hint: He returned from Munich promising peace.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: What German word describes the union of Germany and Austria in 1938?
questions.hint: It begins with 'A' and means 'connection' or 'union'.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: In which year did German troops march into the Rhineland?
questions.hint: It happened two years before the union with Austria.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which treaty had forbidden Germany from uniting with Austria?
questions.hint: It was signed after the First World War.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: The Sudetenland was part of which country before 1938?
questions.hint: Germany claimed it because many German speakers lived there.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which country was NOT invited to the Munich Conference in September 1938?
questions.hint: It was the country whose land was being discussed.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: What did the Munich Agreement allow Germany to do?
questions.hint: It concerned a border region with many German speakers.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: In March 1939, what did Germany do that showed appeasement had failed?
options: Signed a peace treaty with Britain
questions.hint: Hitler had promised he wanted only the German-speaking areas.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which agreement of August 1939 meant Germany would not face the USSR if it invaded Poland?
questions.hint: It was a surprise deal between two very different regimes.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: On what date did Britain declare war on Germany?
questions.hint: It came two days after Germany invaded Poland.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which was a reason why many British people supported appeasement?
options: Memories of the huge losses of the First World War
Britain's army was much larger than Germany's
Britain had already signed an alliance with the USSR
Most people wanted to fight Germany immediately
questions.answer: Memories of the huge losses of the First World War
questions.hint: Think about what had happened only twenty years earlier.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which is a common argument AGAINST appeasement?
options: It encouraged Hitler to make bigger demands
It gave Britain no time to rearm
It made the USSR an ally of Britain
questions.answer: It encouraged Hitler to make bigger demands
questions.hint: Think about what Hitler did after each success.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Which aim of Hitler's foreign policy meant 'living space' for Germans in the east?
questions.hint: It is a German word made of 'life' and 'space'.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: Explain one reason why Chamberlain followed a policy of appeasement.
questions.hint: Consider public opinion, the state of Britain's armed forces, or views about the Treaty of Versailles.

questions.subject: hist
questions.q: 'Appeasement was a sensible policy in 1938.' Give one argument for and one argument against this view.
questions.hint: Think about time to rearm versus what Hitler did next.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 5⁰.
questions.hint: Any non-zero number to the power zero gives the same answer.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 2⁻³. Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.hint: A negative index means take the reciprocal.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 10⁻². Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.hint: Find 10², then take the reciprocal.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: What is x⁻¹ equal to?
questions.hint: A power of -1 gives the reciprocal.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 9^(1/2).
questions.hint: A power of 1/2 means a square root.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 8^(1/3).
questions.hint: A power of 1/3 means a cube root.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate (1/2)⁻².
questions.hint: Flip the fraction, then square it.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 3⁻² × 3⁴.
questions.hint: Add the indices first.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 16^(-1/2). Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.hint: Do the root, then deal with the negative sign.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 32^(1/5).
questions.hint: Which number multiplied by itself five times gives 32?

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 4^(3/2).
questions.hint: Take the square root first, then cube.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 27^(2/3).
questions.hint: Cube root first, then square.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate 1000^(-1/3). Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.hint: Find the cube root of 1000 first.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Which is equal to 64^(5/6)?
questions.hint: Find the sixth root of 64, then raise to the power 5.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Evaluate (8/27)^(-2/3). Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.hint: Flip the fraction for the negative index, then cube root and square.

questions.subject: math
questions.q: Explain why a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero number a, using the rule for dividing powers.
questions.hint: Think about what aⁿ ÷ aⁿ equals in two different ways.

questions.subject: pt
questions.q: O que é uma resenha crítica?
options: Um texto que apresenta e avalia uma obra
Um texto que só conta o final de uma história

books.title: O Verão do Outro Lado do Vidro
books.premise: Já adulto, Davi relembra o verão em que, aos onze anos, passou as férias na casa da avó numa cidadezinha do interior e descobriu que seu reflexo no velho espelho do corredor tinha vontade própria. chapters.title: Capítulo 1: O espelho do corredor
chapters.synopsis: Davi, já adulto, relembra o verão em que, aos onze anos, foi passar as férias na casa da avó e viu seu reflexo piscar sozinho.
chapters.text:
Hoje, quando passo diante de qualquer espelho, ainda me lembro daquele verão. Eu tinha onze anos e meus pais me mandaram passar as férias inteiras na casa da minha avó Lurdes, em Vargem do Sino, uma cidadezinha onde o ônibus chegava só duas vezes por dia e o relógio da igreja vivia atrasado.
A casa era comprida, cheia de portas que rangiam, e tinha um corredor escuro que ligava a sala à cozinha. No meio desse corredor ficava um espelho enorme, de moldura dourada e descascada, mais velho do que a própria avó. Ela dizia que ele tinha vindo de navio, embrulhado em cobertores, mas a avó gostava de inventar origens nobres para as coisas mais simples.
Naquela época, eu ainda não conhecia ninguém na cidade. Meus amigos estavam longe, a televisão da avó só pegava um canal, cheio de chuviscos, e as tardes pareciam ter o dobro de horas. Eu andava pela casa abrindo gavetas, contando as tábuas do assoalho e espiando o quintal, onde as galinhas ciscavam sem pressa nenhuma. Era um tédio tão grande que eu chegava a ouvir o tique-taque do relógio da sala de qualquer cômodo.
Na primeira noite, eu fui buscar um copo de água e parei diante do espelho. Estava cansado da viagem, com o cabelo grudado de suor e a camiseta do avesso. Fiz uma careta para mim mesmo, como qualquer menino faria. O menino do espelho fez a mesma careta. Até aí, nada de estranho.
Então eu me virei para ir embora e, com o canto do olho, vi: o reflexo continuou parado, olhando para mim. E piscou. Só um olho, devagar, como quem divide um segredo.
Lembro que o copo quase escorregou da minha mão. Voltei a encarar o espelho, e lá estava ele, imitando cada movimento meu, obediente como todo reflexo deve ser. Levantei o braço direito; ele levantou o esquerdo. Abri a boca; ele abriu também. Fiquei ali um tempão, esperando que errasse de novo. Ele não errou.
Hoje, já adulto, não sei dizer se aquilo aconteceu mesmo ou se foi o cansaço de um menino com saudade de casa. A memória é uma gaveta bagunçada: a gente guarda as coisas de um jeito e, anos depois, encontra de outro. Mas sei que, naquela noite, voltei para a cama com o coração disparado e fiquei ouvindo os grilos lá fora, pensando que talvez houvesse alguém do outro lado do vidro.
Na manhã seguinte, a avó me serviu café com leite e pão de queijo. Perguntou se eu tinha dormido bem. Eu disse que sim. Pensei em contar sobre o espelho, mas imaginei a cara dela, meio rindo, meio preocupada, dizendo que menino da cidade grande tem a cabeça cheia de televisão.
Então decidi guardar o segredo. Afinal, se o menino do espelho tinha piscado só para mim, era porque o assunto era entre nós dois.

chapters.title: Capítulo 2: O milho debulhado
chapters.synopsis: O reflexo se oferece para fazer a tarefa de Davi enquanto ele vai ao rio, e deixa uma assinatura curiosa.
chapters.text:
Durante três dias, o menino do espelho se comportou como qualquer reflexo bem-educado. Eu passava pelo corredor dez, vinte vezes, e ele só me imitava. Comecei a achar que tinha sonhado.
No quarto dia, a avó me entregou uma bacia cheia de espigas e um banquinho. “Debulha esse milho todo, que amanhã é dia de fazer pamonha”, disse ela, e foi para o quintal cuidar das galinhas. Eram umas trinta espigas. Do lado de fora, os meninos da rua gritavam meu nome, chamando para nadar no rio.
Olhei para aquela montanha de espigas e calculei que levaria a tarde inteira. Meus dedos já doíam só de imaginar. Tentei debulhar a primeira com pressa, girando a espiga entre as mãos como a avó fazia, mas os grãos espirravam para todos os lados e caíam no chão, menos na bacia. Lá fora, os gritos ficavam mais altos, e depois mais distantes, como se a turma estivesse indo embora sem mim.
Arrastei a bacia até o corredor, só para ter onde reclamar sozinho. Sentei de frente para o espelho e falei, mais para mim do que para ele: “Bem que você podia fazer isso no meu lugar.”
O reflexo sorriu. Eu não estava sorrindo.
Depois, sem pressa, ele estendeu a mão, como quem pede uma espiga. Fiquei paralisado. Então, com a coragem que só aparece quando a gente quer muito fugir de uma obrigação, encostei uma espiga no vidro. Ela não bateu no espelho: atravessou, macia, como se entrasse na água. Do outro lado, o menino a segurou e começou a debulhar.
Não pensei duas vezes. Empurrei a bacia inteira para dentro do vidro, peguei meu calção e corri para o rio.
Foi uma tarde perfeita. Pulei da pedra mais alta, apostei corrida com o Tito, filho da vizinha, e voltei com o nariz queimado de sol. Só quando avistei o portão da avó foi que senti um frio na barriga. E se o milho não estivesse pronto?
Estava. A bacia esperava no corredor, cheia de grãos amarelos, e as espigas peladas estavam empilhadas num canto, todas iguais. A avó, que já tinha voltado do quintal, olhou o trabalho e disse que nunca tinha visto milho tão bem debulhado.
Só à noite, sozinho, percebi um detalhe. Em cima dos grãos, alguém tinha arrumado alguns deles formando letras: IVAD. Demorei um pouco para entender. Era o meu nome, escrito ao contrário, como aparece num espelho.
Olhei para o reflexo. Ele estava me imitando, sério, obediente. Mas eu tinha certeza de que, por dentro, estava rindo.
Hoje penso que talvez eu mesmo tenha debulhado aquele milho, morrendo de preguiça, e inventado o resto para tornar a tarde mais bonita. A memória gosta de enfeitar. Mas aquelas quatro letras eu ainda vejo, nítidas, sobre o amarelo dos grãos.

chapters.synopsis: Davi aceita trocar de lugar com o reflexo por uma tarde e descobre como é o mundo invertido do espelho.
chapters.text:
Depois do milho, o menino do espelho e eu passamos a conversar. Não com palavras: ele não tinha voz. Mas escrevia com o dedo no vidro embaçado, sempre de trás para frente, e eu aprendi a ler depressa. Ele assinava IVAD, e eu passei a chamá-lo assim.
Um dia, Ivad escreveu: “Troca comigo?”
Eu entendi na hora. Ele queria sair. Queria sentir o sol de verdade, correr na rua de terra, comer a goiabada da avó. E, em troca, eu poderia conhecer o lado de lá.
Passei a noite inteira virando de um lado para o outro na cama. Imaginava o que haveria do outro lado do vidro: um quintal ao contrário, uma cidade inteira de cabeça para baixo, quem sabe outro menino que, lá, fosse eu. De manhã, comi depressa, quase sem sentir o gosto do pão, e voltei ao corredor antes que a coragem fosse embora. Hesitei. E se eu ficasse preso? Mas a curiosidade, aos onze anos, pesa mais do que o medo.
Encostei a palma da mão no vidro, ele encostou a dele do outro lado, e trocamos.
O mundo do espelho era a casa da avó, só que ao contrário. A porta da cozinha ficava à esquerda, o relógio da parede andava para trás, e o retrato do meu avô sorria com o lado errado da boca. Pela janela, vi o rio correndo de volta para a nascente. Até o cheiro era diferente: um cheiro de coisa guardada, de roupa esquecida no armário.
O mais estranho era o silêncio. Lá dentro não havia grilos, nem rádio, nem galinhas. Eu falava e minha voz não saía. Entendi, então, por que Ivad escrevia em vez de falar.
Fiquei a tarde inteira observando, pelo vidro, o que acontecia do lado de cá. Vi Ivad, com a minha cara e as minhas roupas, comer três fatias de goiabada. Vi a avó passar por ele e fazer um carinho na cabeça dele, achando que era eu. Senti uma pontada de ciúme que não sabia explicar.
Quando o sol começou a baixar, Ivad voltou ao corredor, ofegante e feliz. Encostamos as mãos e trocamos de novo. O barulho do mundo voltou de uma vez, como quando a gente tira a cabeça de dentro da água.
No vidro embaçado, ele escreveu: “Obrigado.” E, embaixo, uma coisa que me deixou pensando a noite inteira: “Aqui fora é bom porque tem você.”
Hoje, adulto, sei que os espelhos não guardam mundos. Mas aprendi, naquela tarde, que ver a própria vida de fora é estranho: a gente percebe o carinho que recebe e nem sempre nota.

chapters.title: Capítulo 4: A pipa e a briga
chapters.synopsis: No festival de pipas, Davi briga com o amigo Tito, e Ivad resolve a situação de um jeito que Davi não conseguiria.
chapters.text:
No último sábado de janeiro, Vargem do Sino fazia o festival de pipas no morro do cruzeiro. Eu e o Tito passamos a semana construindo uma pipa juntos: varetas de bambu, papel de seda vermelho e uma rabiola tão comprida que dava duas voltas no quintal.
No dia do festival, o vento estava perfeito. A pipa subiu bonita, e foi o Tito quem segurou a linha na hora em que os jurados passaram. Ganhamos o primeiro lugar. O prêmio era um carretel novo, de madeira envernizada, e o jurado o entregou ao Tito.
Eu fiquei furioso. A ideia da rabiola tinha sido minha. As varetas, fui eu que cortei. Na volta, discutimos no meio da rua. Eu disse coisas feias. Ele disse coisas feias. Cada um foi para sua casa batendo o portão.
Passei o resto da tarde fingindo que não me importava. Joguei bola sozinho contra o muro, dei milho às galinhas sem que ninguém pedisse, arrumei a gaveta de meias. Nada adiantava. Toda vez que eu fechava os olhos, via o carretel brilhando nas mãos do Tito e ouvia, de novo, as palavras feias que eu tinha dito. O pior é que eu sabia que algumas delas não eram verdade.
À noite, sentei no chão do corredor, emburrado. No vidro, Ivad escreveu: “Você sabe que ele também trabalhou.”
Eu sabia. Mas sabia também que não conseguiria pedir desculpas. As palavras ficavam presas na garganta, duras como caroço de manga.
“Eu vou”, escreveu Ivad.
Trocamos de lugar mais uma vez. Do lado de dentro, vi meu reflexo atravessar o corredor e sair pela porta da frente. Não pude ouvir a conversa, mas vi, pela janela invertida, Ivad parado no portão do Tito, falando com calma e gesticulando com a mão esquerda. Vi o Tito cruzar os braços, depois descruzar, depois rir. No fim, os dois se abraçaram.
Quando trocamos de volta, Ivad escreveu só: “Amanhã vocês vão soltar a pipa juntos. O carretel fica uma semana com cada um.”
Fiquei aliviado e, ao mesmo tempo, envergonhado. Era como se existisse uma versão de mim mais corajosa, mais gentil, que sabia fazer as coisas que eu não sabia. E essa versão morava num espelho.
No dia seguinte, o Tito me recebeu sorrindo. “Gostei do que você disse ontem”, falou. “Nunca pensei que você fosse falar aquilo.” Eu sorri de volta, sem saber exatamente o que eu tinha dito.
Hoje, quando lembro dessa história, desconfio que fui eu mesmo até o portão do Tito, tremendo, e que precisei imaginar outro menino para ter coragem. Às vezes, a gente inventa um duplo para fazer aquilo que ainda não acredita ser capaz de fazer.

chapters.title: Capítulo 5: O que a avó sabia
chapters.synopsis: Numa noite de chuva, a avó conta uma lembrança de infância que deixa Davi desconfiado de que ela conhece o segredo do espelho.
chapters.text:
Em fevereiro, choveu por quatro dias seguidos. A luz acabava toda tarde, e a avó acendia lamparinas que faziam as sombras dançarem nas paredes. Sem rio, sem rua e sem Tito, eu passava horas no corredor, conversando com Ivad pelo vidro embaçado.
Naqueles dias, ele me ensinou a jogar uma espécie de jogo da velha ao contrário, em que perdia quem fizesse a linha primeiro. Também desenhávamos mapas de tesouros imaginários, ele do lado de lá, eu do lado de cá, e as linhas se encontravam no meio do vidro. A avó passava, olhava os rabiscos e não dizia nada. Só uma vez comentou que eu estava gastando muito pano para limpar espelho.
Numa dessas noites, a avó apareceu com duas canecas de chocolate quente e sentou no banquinho ao meu lado. Ficou um tempo olhando o espelho, em silêncio. Depois disse:
“Sabe que esse espelho já foi da minha mãe? Quando eu era menina, tinha medo de passar por ele à noite.”
Perguntei por quê. Ela riu.
“Porque eu achava que havia uma menina lá dentro. Uma menina igualzinha a mim, só que mais corajosa. Ela fazia as coisas que eu não tinha coragem de fazer. Eu chamava ela de Sedrul.”
Senti o chocolate esfriar na minha mão. Sedrul. Era Lurdes ao contrário.
“E o que aconteceu com ela?”, perguntei, quase sem voz.
A avó deu de ombros. “Eu cresci. Um dia, olhei no espelho e vi só eu mesma. Fiquei triste uns dias. Depois entendi que ela não tinha ido embora: tinha vindo morar aqui dentro.” E bateu de leve no próprio peito.
Ficamos calados um tempo, ouvindo a chuva no telhado. Eu queria perguntar se ela sabia de Ivad, mas não perguntei. Tinha medo de que, se eu falasse o nome dele em voz alta, alguma coisa se quebrasse.
Antes de ir dormir, a avó passou a mão no meu cabelo e disse: “Espelho velho guarda muita coisa, Davi. Mas só devolve o que a gente leva até ele.”
Fiquei acordado pensando nisso. Quando finalmente olhei para o corredor, Ivad tinha escrito no vidro, com letras miúdas: “Ela sabe.”
Hoje, muitos anos depois, fico pensando se a avó realmente teve uma Sedrul ou se inventou aquela história naquela noite, só para mim. Talvez tenha percebido um neto sozinho, falando com o espelho, e tenha escolhido não rir nem ralhar, mas fazer companhia. Seja como for, foi a coisa mais bonita que alguém poderia ter me dito naquele verão.

chapters.title: Capítulo 6: O reflexo comum
chapters.synopsis: Uma manhã, Ivad não responde mais, e Davi precisa enfrentar sozinho um dia difícil.
chapters.text:
Na última semana de férias, acordei cedo e fui direto ao corredor, como fazia todos os dias. Bati de leve no vidro. Meu reflexo bateu também, exatamente ao mesmo tempo. Soprei o espelho para embaçá-lo e esperei as letras ao contrário. Nada.
Tentei piscar um olho só. O reflexo piscou junto, com o olho certo, sem atraso. Fiz caretas, escrevi perguntas, chamei o nome dele baixinho. O menino do espelho apenas me copiava, perfeito, comum, como o reflexo de qualquer pessoa em qualquer casa.
Passei a manhã inteira angustiado. Olhei no espelho do banheiro, na janela da sala, até no fundo da panela de alumínio. Em todos, só havia eu.
Para piorar, era o dia que eu mais temia. A avó tinha marcado de eu ajudar a dona Cida, a vizinha da frente, a carregar caixas para a festa da igreja. Dona Cida era brava, falava alto e reclamava de tudo. Em outros tempos, eu teria pedido a Ivad para ir no meu lugar.
Voltei ao corredor uma última vez, quase implorando. Encostei a palma da mão no vidro e esperei sentir aquela maciez de água, o caminho para o outro lado. Mas o espelho estava frio e duro, como qualquer espelho. Meu reflexo também encostou a mão, mas era só um gesto copiado, sem vontade própria. Pela primeira vez naquele verão, eu me senti realmente sozinho na casa da avó.
Fiquei parado na porta, com vontade de inventar uma dor de barriga. Então lembrei da pipa, do portão do Tito, do milho arrumado em letras. Lembrei da avó dizendo que a menina do espelho tinha vindo morar dentro dela.
Atravessei a rua.
Carreguei caixas a manhã inteira. Dona Cida reclamou do meu jeito de segurar, da minha pressa, do meu tênis sujo. Mas, lá pelas tantas, quando eu equilibrei sozinho uma pilha de pratos sem quebrar nenhum, ela parou e disse: “Esse menino é jeitoso.” E me deu um pedaço de bolo de fubá ainda quente.
Voltei para casa no fim da tarde, cansado e estranhamente contente. Passei pelo corredor e, por hábito, olhei para o espelho. O reflexo me olhou de volta, sério. Depois, devagar, com o mesmo jeito daquela primeira noite, piscou um olho só.
Não escreveu nada. Não precisava.
Hoje entendo que aquele dia foi uma despedida. Ivad tinha ficado comigo enquanto eu precisei dele, e foi embora quando percebeu que eu conseguia atravessar a rua sozinho. Ou, talvez, quem foi embora tenha sido o menino que precisava de um duplo.

chapters.title: Capítulo 7: O espelho hoje
chapters.synopsis: Já adulto, Davi recebe o espelho da avó e, diante da filha pequena, pensa no que a memória guarda e no que a imaginação cria.
chapters.text:
Muitos anos se passaram. Cresci, estudei, mudei de cidade algumas vezes. Voltei a Vargem do Sino em muitas férias, mas nunca mais vi Ivad. O espelho continuava no corredor, cada vez mais descascado, e meu reflexo me obedecia com uma disciplina quase entediante.
Quando a avó Lurdes decidiu se mudar para um apartamento pequeno, perto da minha tia, ela me chamou para escolher alguma coisa da casa. Não precisei pensar. “O espelho”, eu disse. Ela sorriu como quem já sabia a resposta.
Trouxemos o espelho embrulhado em cobertores, como ela dizia que ele tinha chegado ao Brasil. Hoje ele está no corredor do meu apartamento, entre a sala e a cozinha, porque não consegui imaginá-lo em outro lugar.
No começo, os vizinhos do prédio estranharam aquele móvel antigo, de moldura dourada e descascada, no meio de um apartamento moderno. Um deles chegou a perguntar se eu queria o telefone de alguém para restaurar a moldura. Agradeci e disse que não. As falhas no dourado, as manchas escuras nos cantos do vidro, tudo aquilo fazia parte da história. Restaurar seria como apagar um pedaço da memória.
Minha filha tem sete anos. Outro dia, eu a vi parada diante do espelho, fazendo caretas, exatamente como eu fazia. De repente, ela correu até mim, com os olhos arregalados.
“Pai! A menina do espelho piscou pra mim!”
Senti o tempo dobrar, como uma folha de papel em que duas pontas distantes se encontram. Eu poderia ter dito que era impossível, que reflexos não piscam sozinhos, que ela devia estar cansada. Em vez disso, me ajoelhei e perguntei: “E você piscou de volta?”
Ela pensou um pouco e disse que não. Ficou com medo. Eu disse que, da próxima vez, ela podia tentar.
Naquela noite, depois que ela dormiu, fiquei um tempo diante do espelho. Pensei em tudo o que contei nestas páginas: o milho, a troca de lugar, a pipa, a chuva, a dona Cida. Não sei quanto disso aconteceu do jeito que lembro. A memória não é um arquivo fiel; é mais como uma conversa entre o menino que eu fui e o homem que eu sou. Cada vez que conto essa história, um dos dois acrescenta alguma coisa.
Talvez Ivad nunca tenha existido. Talvez tenha sido apenas o nome que dei à parte de mim que ainda não sabia ter coragem. Mas, de algum modo, ele continua existindo agora, porque eu o lembro, e porque minha filha, sem saber de nada, encontrou alguém parecido do outro lado do vidro.
Antes de apagar a luz do corredor, olhei meu reflexo nos olhos. Por um segundo, achei que ele ia piscar. Não piscou. Eu sorri mesmo assim.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Everyone Hates the New Timetable
chapters.synopsis: Tamsin joins the Saltmarsh Point school newspaper and is told to test a bold headline before it is printed.
chapters.text:
The newspaper room at Saltmarsh Point Academy smelled of toner and old biscuits. Tamsin Varga had walked past it for two years before she finally knocked on the door on a wet Tuesday in November.
"New recruit?" asked a tall boy with ink on his fingers. "I'm Ravi. Editor-in-chief, unpaid. That's Joaquim, he does photos and complains." Joaquim lifted a hand without looking up from his camera.
Their teacher adviser, Mr Pellow, was pinning a draft front page to the corkboard. In huge letters it said: EVERYONE HATES THE NEW TIMETABLE.
"Is that true?" Tamsin asked before she could stop herself.
Mr Pellow turned round, delighted. "Excellent question. That is exactly what this paper is for. Ravi, where did the headline come from?"
Ravi shrugged. "Everyone in my form was moaning about it. Lunch is twenty minutes later now and the buses leave before after-school clubs finish."
"How many people are in your form?" said Mr Pellow.
"Twenty-six."
"And how many students are in the school?"
"About nine hundred," Ravi admitted.
Mr Pellow wrote a sentence on the whiteboard: To what extent do students dislike the new timetable? "In exams," he said, "you will meet questions like this. 'To what extent' means you never answer simply yes or no. You weigh the evidence on both sides and then decide how far the statement is true. Tamsin, you asked the question, so you can test it."
For the next three days Tamsin carried a clipboard everywhere. She asked one student from every form group the same three questions, and she was careful not to say what she thought herself. Joaquim took photographs of the bus queue. Ravi, a little grumpily, interviewed the kitchen staff.
On Friday they spread the results across the table. Of the forty-two students Tamsin had asked, twenty-five disliked the later lunch. But eleven of them said they liked the longer morning lessons, because science practicals no longer had to be rushed. Six students had no opinion at all. The kitchen staff said the later lunch meant fewer students were hungry by the last lesson. The bus photographs, however, were hard to argue with: a long line of students leaving clubs early.
"So," said Mr Pellow, "is the headline true?"
Tamsin looked at the numbers. "Partly. More than half of the people I asked dislike lunch being later, so there is real evidence for it. But 'everyone' is false. Some students like parts of the change, and the clubs problem is about buses, not really the timetable itself."
Ravi groaned, crossed out the headline and wrote a new one: MOST STUDENTS UNHAPPY WITH LATE LUNCH, BUT LONGER LESSONS WIN SOME FANS.
"It's longer," he said.
"It's truer," said Joaquim.
Mr Pellow smiled and handed Tamsin a key to the newspaper room. As she left, she noticed an old leather notebook on the top shelf, its spine stamped with a single word: LEDGER. She meant to ask about it, but the bell rang, and the question stayed with her all weekend.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Lighthouse That Was Never Lit
chapters.synopsis: A local legend claims the Saltmarsh lighthouse was never used, and the team tests it against the old ledger.
chapters.text:
On Monday Tamsin finally asked about the leather notebook.
"Ah, the Ledger," said Mr Pellow, lifting it down carefully. "Every editor since this paper began has written in it. One rule: before a big claim goes into print, you write it here, with the evidence for and against, and your verdict."
The first page, in faded blue ink, was dated forty years earlier. Tamsin turned the pages slowly. Some verdicts said TRUE, some FALSE, and many said PARTLY TRUE, with careful notes underneath.
Ravi was already pacing. "Perfect timing. The town council wants to turn the lighthouse into a café. And everyone knows the lighthouse was never actually lit. It was built and then the ships changed route. My grandad told me. It's the most famous fact in Saltmarsh."
"Then it should be easy to check," said Tamsin.
It was not easy. The library had a book of local history, but it simply repeated the story without saying where it came from. Joaquim found a postcard from long ago that showed the lighthouse with a bright beam drawn across the sky. "That proves it was lit," he said.
"A drawing on a postcard proves someone drew a beam," said Tamsin. "Artists add things."
On Thursday the three of them visited the harbour museum. A volunteer named Mrs Abara led them to a glass case containing a keeper's logbook. Each page listed the date, the weather and the words 'lamp lit at sunset'. The entries ran for just under three years and then stopped.
"So it was lit," said Ravi, sounding almost disappointed.
"For a while," said Mrs Abara. "After three years a new lighthouse opened further down the coast, on the point where the shipping lane actually ran. This one was switched off. People forgot it ever worked, and the story grew."
Back in the newspaper room, Tamsin opened the Ledger and drew two columns.
For the claim, she wrote: the local history book; Ravi's grandad; the fact that the lighthouse was closed quickly, which may have started the story.
Against the claim, she wrote: the keeper's logbook, written at the time by someone who was there; the museum's explanation of the new lighthouse.
Then she paused over the postcard. "Where does this go?"
"Against," said Joaquim.
"I don't think it goes anywhere," said Tamsin. "It isn't reliable either way." She wrote it at the bottom under a third heading: Weak evidence.
Her verdict took longer. Finally she wrote: MOSTLY FALSE. The lighthouse was lit for nearly three years. The legend is true only in that it was used for a much shorter time than planned.
Ravi read it twice. "My grandad is going to argue with this."
"Then bring him the logbook," said Tamsin. "If he has better evidence, we'll change the verdict."
That Saturday Ravi did exactly that. He came back on Monday grinning. His grandad had read every page, frowned, and then said that the logbook was better evidence than a story told on the harbour wall. He had also asked if he could write a letter to the paper about it.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Seagull Problem
chapters.synopsis: A café owner says seagulls are taking over the seafront, and the team counts birds to find out.
chapters.text:
The next claim arrived by email from the owner of the Driftwood Café. Mr Henshaw wanted the paper to print a warning: SEAGULLS ARE TAKING OVER SALTMARSH. He said gulls had stolen three sandwiches from his customers in a single afternoon, and that there were 'ten times more birds than last year'.
"Ten times," Joaquim repeated. "That's a lot of gulls."
"It's a lot of claim," said Tamsin.
Ravi had a plan. "We count them. Same place, same time, every day for a week."
Joaquim pointed out a problem at once. "If we only count outside the café, we'll find loads. That's where the food is."
So they chose three spots: the café terrace, the quiet end of the beach and the harbour wall. Each lunchtime for a week they counted for ten minutes at each spot and wrote the numbers in a table. Joaquim photographed every count so that nobody could argue later.
The results surprised them. Outside the café there were between twenty and thirty-five gulls every day. At the harbour wall there were around fifteen. At the quiet end of the beach there were often fewer than five.
"So they're not taking over the whole town," said Ravi. "They're taking over one café."
But Tamsin was still thinking about the 'ten times more' part. They had no count from last year, so they could not test it directly. Then Mrs Abara from the museum mentioned that a local bird club counted gulls on the harbour wall every autumn. Their records showed about twelve birds at the same spot the year before.
"Twelve last year, about fifteen this year," said Tamsin. "That's more, but nowhere near ten times."
They went to see Mr Henshaw. He listened, arms folded, while they explained.
"Well, it feels like ten times more," he said.
"We believe you that it's worse at your café," said Tamsin carefully. "Our counts show that too. But the evidence suggests the birds are coming to where the food is, not that the town is full of them."
Mr Henshaw was quiet for a moment. Then he admitted that he had started leaving the bins open behind the kitchen in the summer, because the lid was broken.
That evening Tamsin wrote in the Ledger. For: high counts at the café; three stolen sandwiches; the owner's experience. Against: low counts on the quiet beach; the bird club's figures, which show only a small rise; a likely local cause, the open bins.
Verdict: LARGELY FALSE as a statement about the town. TRUE that one area has a serious gull problem, probably caused by food waste.
The article that Friday was headlined: GULLS FLOCK TO FOOD, NOT TO SALTMARSH. Below it was a short box with advice on keeping bins closed. A week later Mr Henshaw sent a photograph of his new bin lid and a free cake voucher for the newspaper team.
"Is accepting cake from someone we wrote about allowed?" asked Joaquim.
Mr Pellow thought about it. "Write it in the Ledger," he said. "Then share the cake with the whole class."

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Phone Ban Made Us Happier
chapters.synopsis: The school claims its phone ban has made students happier, and Tamsin finds the survey is less simple than it looks.
chapters.text:
In January the head teacher's newsletter made a bold announcement: SINCE THE PHONE BAN, OUR STUDENTS ARE HAPPIER. It quoted a survey in which sixty per cent of students said they were 'happier at break time' than before.
Ravi wanted to print it on the front page. "It's the school's own survey. Surely that's reliable."
"Maybe," said Tamsin. "Who wrote the questions?"
That turned out to be a good place to start. The survey had been sent out by the student council. Its first question read: Do you agree that break times are more sociable now that everyone is talking instead of staring at screens?
"That question basically tells you the answer," said Joaquim.
"It's a leading question," said Tamsin. "It makes agreeing feel like the normal thing to do."
They also discovered that only students who opened the newsletter email had replied: about one in five of the school. Tamsin wondered whether students who liked the ban were more likely to answer.
Still, she didn't want to dismiss the claim just because the survey had problems. "Bad evidence doesn't mean the claim is false," she reminded the others. "It just means we don't know yet."
So they looked for other evidence. The school nurse, who would not discuss individual students, said that fewer students had come to her office upset about online arguments during the school day. The librarian said the library was busier at lunchtime. Joaquim photographed the playground at break and found far more groups playing games or chatting than he remembered from the autumn.
Then Ravi interviewed a group of Year 11 students, who were far less positive. Several said they felt anxious without their phones because they could not check messages from home. One said she was happier at break but more stressed at the end of the day, when twenty notifications arrived at once.
Tamsin designed a fairer survey. The questions were neutral: How do you feel at break time compared with last term? with options from 'much worse' to 'much better'. Mr Pellow helped them send it to every tutor group to be filled in during registration, so almost everyone answered.
The results were mixed but clear. Just over half said they felt better at break. About a third said there was no difference. Around one in seven said they felt worse, and most of those were older students.
In the Ledger, Tamsin wrote: For: fairer survey shows most students feel better at break; fewer upset visits to the nurse; busier library; photographs. Against: original survey used a leading question and a small sample; a sizeable minority, mostly older students, feel worse; 'happier' at break may not mean happier overall.
Verdict: TRUE TO A LARGE EXTENT for break times, especially for younger students. NOT PROVEN for happiness in general.
The head teacher was not thrilled by the article at first. Then she invited Tamsin to a meeting with the student council to discuss letting older students check phones at the end of lunch. "Your article gave us a better question to ask," she said.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Is the Old Pier Unsafe?
chapters.synopsis: After a photograph of a broken plank spreads online, the team weighs a rumour against an engineer's report.
chapters.text:
The photograph appeared on a local social media page on a Sunday night: a broken plank on the old pier, with the caption THIS PIER IS A DEATH TRAP. By Monday morning it had been shared hundreds of times, and parents at the school gate were talking about nothing else.
"We have to cover this," said Ravi. "It's the biggest story in town."
"Then we have to be the most careful," said Tamsin.
Joaquim studied the picture on his phone. "Look at the shadows. The sun's coming from the left and it's quite low. And see that railing? It's painted green. I'm sure the railings were repainted blue last spring."
That evening they walked down to the pier. The railings were indeed blue. Near the end they found the plank from the photograph, or one very like it, but it had been replaced with new, pale wood. A small metal notice, half hidden by a lamppost, said: Repairs completed in October.
"So the photo is old," said Ravi.
"Probably old," Tamsin corrected. "We can't be completely sure. But it doesn't show the pier as it is now."
The council's website listed an engineer's inspection from the summer. Mr Pellow helped them read it. The report said the structure was 'sound', but it also listed eleven planks needing replacement and recommended that the far end be inspected again after winter storms.
"So it isn't a death trap," said Joaquim.
"But it isn't perfect either," said Tamsin. "And the report is from before the storms in November."
They decided to ask the council directly. A spokesperson replied by email that a second inspection was already booked for the following week. She also admitted that the warning signs about high waves had been blown away and not yet replaced.
Tamsin spread everything out on the table. For the claim that the pier was unsafe: the broken plank in the photograph, if it was recent; eleven planks needing work; missing warning signs; the storms since the last inspection. Against: the photograph was almost certainly taken before the repairs; the engineer had called the structure sound; a new inspection was already planned.
Ravi wanted a dramatic headline. Tamsin wanted a cautious one. They argued for twenty minutes.
"If we say it's safe and someone gets hurt, that's terrible," said Ravi.
"If we say it's a death trap and it isn't, we're just as bad as the post we're checking," said Tamsin.
In the end they agreed on: PIER PHOTO IS OUT OF DATE, BUT STORM CHECK STILL NEEDED. The article explained how they had worked out that the photograph was old, quoted the engineer's report, and pointed out the missing wave signs.
The verdict in the Ledger read: MOSTLY FALSE as stated. 'Death trap' is not supported by the evidence. However, some concern is reasonable until the post-storm inspection is complete.
Two days after the paper came out, new wave warning signs appeared on the pier. Nobody from the council mentioned the article, but Joaquim took a photograph of the signs anyway, and this time he wrote the date on the back.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: It Was the Referee's Fault
chapters.synopsis: After a painful football defeat, Ravi is sure the referee cost the school the cup, and he has to test his own claim.
chapters.text:
Saltmarsh Point lost the county football final 2–1, and Ravi took it personally. He had been in the crowd, shouting until his voice gave out, and on Monday he burst into the newspaper room with a headline already written: REFEREE ROBS SALTMARSH OF THE CUP.
Tamsin and Joaquim exchanged a look.
"Don't," said Ravi. "I know what you're going to say. But I saw it. Their winning goal was offside, and he didn't give us a penalty when Kofi was pushed over. Everyone saw it."
"Everyone in our stand," said Joaquim quietly.
Mr Pellow leaned back in his chair. "Ravi, you've helped test four claims this term. Do you want to test this one, or do you want someone else to?"
Ravi hesitated. "I'll do it," he said at last. "Properly."
It was harder than he expected. The match had been filmed by a parent from the halfway line, and Joaquim had taken photographs from behind the goal. Ravi watched the winning goal again and again. From the side, the attacker looked level with the last defender. Joaquim's photograph, taken from a different angle, made it look as if he might be slightly ahead.
"I can't tell," Ravi admitted. "It's really close."
The penalty claim was clearer. The video showed a defender's arm on Kofi's shoulder as they both chased the ball. Kofi fell. But the coach, when Ravi interviewed her, said she thought it was 'fifty-fifty' and that she had seen worse challenges go unpunished all season.
Then Tamsin asked a question Ravi did not want to hear. "What else happened in the match?"
He looked at his notes. Saltmarsh had missed a penalty in the first half. Their goalkeeper had dropped an easy cross for the opposition's first goal. And the other team had had fourteen shots to Saltmarsh's six.
Ravi was silent for a long time. Then he picked up a pen and opened the Ledger.
For the claim: one goal that may have been offside, impossible to judge clearly from the footage; one possible penalty that was not given, which even the coach called fifty-fifty.
Against: Saltmarsh missed their own penalty; a goalkeeping mistake gave away the first goal; the other team created far more chances; the referee's decisions were close calls rather than obvious errors.
Verdict: LARGELY FALSE. The referee's decisions may have affected the result, but there is not enough evidence to say they caused the defeat. The match was lost for several reasons.
He showed it to Tamsin. "Is that fair?"
"It's fairer than I expected," she said honestly. "Especially from you."
The article ran under the headline: CLOSE CALLS, BUT SALTMARSH BEATEN ON THE DAY. Ravi wrote it himself. Kofi stopped him in the corridor afterwards. Ravi braced himself for an argument, but Kofi only said, "Thanks for mentioning that we kept going after the second goal. Nobody else noticed that."
That evening Ravi told Tamsin that testing his own claim had been the hardest thing he'd done for the paper. "When you really want something to be true," he said, "you stop looking for the bits that aren't."

chapters.title: Chapter 7: To What Extent Is the Paper Fair?
chapters.synopsis: A reader accuses the newspaper itself of being unfair, and the team turns the Ledger on its own work.
chapters.text:
The letter arrived on the last week of term, written in neat capital letters and signed only 'A Year 10 Reader'. It said: YOUR PAPER PRETENDS TO BE FAIR, BUT YOU ONLY CHECK CLAIMS YOU ALREADY DISAGREE WITH.
Ravi read it aloud and laughed. Then he stopped laughing. "Is it true?"
Tamsin was already reaching for the Ledger. "There's only one way to find out."
They went through every entry from the term: the timetable, the lighthouse, the gulls, the phone ban, the pier and the football final. For each one they asked two questions. Who brought us the claim? And did we expect it to be true or false before we started?
The answers were uncomfortable. Ravi had expected the timetable headline to be true, and the football claim had been his own, so the reader was not entirely right. But Tamsin realised that she had doubted the gull claim and the pier claim from the very start. Joaquim pointed out that they had never once checked a claim made by the newspaper itself.
"And every claim came from someone we could easily disagree with," said Joaquim. "A café owner. Social media. The head teacher."
Mr Pellow joined them at the table. "What about the verdicts? Were they fair?"
That question was easier. In every case, they had recorded the evidence on both sides. Several verdicts had partly supported the original claim. They had offered to change the lighthouse verdict if better evidence appeared, and they had listened to people who disagreed with them, such as the Year 11 students in the phone survey.
"So the method was fair," said Tamsin slowly, "but the choice of what to check might not have been."
Ravi frowned. "How do we fix that?"
They spent the rest of the afternoon making three changes. First, a box would appear in every issue inviting readers to send in any claim, including claims about the paper itself. Second, each term they would check at least one statement that the newspaper team already believed. Third, before starting each investigation, they would write down in the Ledger what they expected the verdict to be, so that they could notice if they were only finding what they wanted to find.
Then Tamsin wrote the final entry of the term.
Claim: The paper only checks claims it already disagrees with.
For: most claims came from people outside the team; Tamsin doubted several claims from the start; the paper never checked its own statements.
Against: Ravi expected at least two of the claims to be true; the evidence was recorded fairly on both sides; the team offered to change verdicts if better evidence appeared.
Verdict: PARTLY TRUE. The method was fair, but the choice of claims showed some bias. Changes have been made.
They printed the letter in full, with the verdict underneath. Two days later another envelope arrived, again in neat capitals. It said only: FAIR ENOUGH. CAN I JOIN?
